CHAPTER 19 — क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः (KRODHO'NARTHAKARAKAH)

Introduction — शीर्षकस्य अर्थः (The meaning of the title)

The very title of this chapter is a small Sanskrit lesson. क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः is formed by विसर्ग-सन्धि from two words: क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः. When a visarga (ः) preceded by अ is followed by the vowel अ, the sequence अः becomes ओ and the following अ is elided; the elision is marked in writing by the sign ऽ, called अवग्रह (avagraha). So क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः → क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः, 'Anger is the causer of ruin.' The word अनर्थः (अन् + अर्थः, 'non-good') means calamity, disaster, ruin — the opposite of अर्थ (welfare, purpose, wealth); कारकः means 'the one who makes or causes' (from the root कृ 'to do'). The wise of India have always counted क्रोध among the inner enemies (षड्रिपु — the six foes: काम, क्रोध, लोभ, मोह, मद, मात्सर्य) and warned in a famous maxim: क्रोधो मूलमनर्थानाम् — 'anger is the root of calamities.' In this lesson (NIOS Senior Secondary Sanskrit, Course 309) we study WHY anger ruins us, through the Bhagavad-Gita's celebrated psychological analysis of the 'anger cascade' (2.62–63), an original retelling of a well-known ancient story of hasty anger, and public-domain niti verses on the answering virtue — क्षमा (forgiveness, forbearance).

गीतायां क्रोध-शृङ्खला — The Gita's anger cascade (2.62–63)

Nowhere is the birth and destructive career of anger analysed more precisely than in two verses of the Bhagavad-Gita (Chapter 2, verses 62–63):

ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते ।
सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥ (गीता 2.62)

अन्वयः: विषयान् ध्यायतः पुंसः तेषु सङ्गः उपजायते । सङ्गात् कामः सञ्जायते । कामात् क्रोधः अभिजायते ।
शब्दार्थः: ध्यायतः = of (a man) constantly brooding/contemplating; विषयान् = sense-objects (things of enjoyment); पुंसः = of a man; तेषु = in them; सङ्गः = attachment; उपजायते = arises; सङ्गात् = from attachment; सञ्जायते = is born; कामः = desire, craving; कामात् = from desire; क्रोधः = anger; अभिजायते = is born, springs up.
Translation: For a man who keeps brooding on sense-objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment is born desire; and from (thwarted) desire anger is born.

क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः ।
स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥ (गीता 2.63)

अन्वयः: क्रोधात् संमोहः भवति । संमोहात् स्मृतिविभ्रमः (भवति) । स्मृतिभ्रंशात् बुद्धिनाशः (भवति) । बुद्धिनाशात् (सः) प्रणश्यति ।
शब्दार्थः: क्रोधात् = from anger; भवति = arises, comes to be; संमोहः = delusion, complete confusion; स्मृतिविभ्रमः = bewilderment (wandering) of memory; स्मृतिभ्रंशात् = from the loss/failure of memory; बुद्धिनाशः = destruction of the intellect (the power of discrimination); प्रणश्यति = (he) perishes utterly, is completely ruined.
Translation: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, bewilderment of memory; from failure of memory, destruction of the intellect; and when the intellect is destroyed, the person perishes.

Notice the chain: विषय-ध्यानम् (brooding on objects) → सङ्गः (attachment) → कामः (desire) → क्रोधः (anger, when desire is blocked) → संमोहः (delusion) → स्मृतिविभ्रमः (memory fails — we forget our own lessons and values) → बुद्धिनाशः (judgement is destroyed) → विनाशः (ruin). Anger is not a sudden bolt from the sky; it is grown, link by link, from unchecked brooding and craving. And once it flares, it darkens the mind step by step until the person can no longer tell right from wrong. The practical wisdom is that the chain is most easily broken at its FIRST link — by not letting the mind brood on the object of craving — for at the later links (delusion, memory-loss) we no longer have the clarity to resist.

The Gita adds a stern warning in 16.21:

त्रिविधं नरकस्येदं द्वारं नाशनमात्मनः ।
कामः क्रोधस्तथा लोभस्तस्मादेतत्त्रयं त्यजेत् ॥ (गीता 16.21)

अन्वयः: कामः क्रोधः तथा लोभः — इदं आत्मनः नाशनं त्रिविधं नरकस्य द्वारम् । तस्मात् एतत् त्रयं त्यजेत् ।
शब्दार्थः: त्रिविधम् = three-fold; नरकस्य = of hell; इदम् = this; द्वारम् = gate, door; नाशनम् = destroyer; आत्मनः = of the self; लोभः = greed; तस्मात् = therefore; एतत् त्रयम् = this triad; त्यजेत् = one should abandon.
Translation: Desire, anger and greed — this is the three-fold gate of hell, destructive of the self; therefore one should abandon these three.

कथा — नकुलस्य कथा (An original retelling of an ancient tale of hasty anger)

कस्मिंश्चिद् ग्रामे देवशर्मा नाम ब्राह्मणः स्वभार्यया सह वसति स्म। तयोः एकः शिशुः आसीत्। गृहे एकः विश्वासपात्रं नकुलः अपि पालितः आसीत्। सः नकुलः शिशुं भ्रातरम् इव रक्षति स्म। एकदा ब्राह्मणी जलम् आनेतुं घटं गृहीत्वा नदीं गता। देवशर्मा अपि भिक्षार्थं बहिः गतः। शिशुः एकाकी शय्यायाम् अस्वपत्। तस्मिन् समये एकः कृष्णसर्पः बिलात् निर्गत्य शय्यां प्रति अचलत्। तं दृष्ट्वा नकुलः शीघ्रम् उत्प्लुत्य सर्पेण सह युद्धं कृत्वा तं खण्डशः अमारयत्। एवं सः शिशोः प्राणान् अरक्षत्।

अनन्तरं ब्राह्मणी घटं गृहीत्वा प्रत्यागता। नकुलः प्रसन्नः सन् रक्तलिप्तमुखेन तां प्रति अधावत्। रक्तं दृष्ट्वा ब्राह्मणी 'अनेन दुष्टेन मम पुत्रः भक्षितः!' इति विचिन्त्य क्रोधेन अन्धा अभवत्। सा विचारं विना एव जलपूर्णं घटं नकुलस्य उपरि अक्षिपत्। नकुलः तत्रैव मृतः। ततः सा गृहं प्रविश्य अपश्यत् — शिशुः सुखेन स्वपिति, शय्यायाः समीपे च मृतः सर्पः खण्डशः पतितः अस्ति। तदा सा सत्यं ज्ञात्वा 'हा! मया रक्षकः एव हतः!' इति मुक्तकण्ठं रुदती महता पश्चात्तापेन अदह्यत। किन्तु गतः प्राणः न प्रत्यागच्छति — क्रोधेन कृतं कर्म न प्रतिक्रियते।

शब्दार्थः: विश्वासपात्रम् = worthy of trust; भिक्षार्थम् = for alms; एकाकी = alone; बिलात् = from its hole; उत्प्लुत्य = leaping up; खण्डशः = to pieces; रक्तलिप्तमुखेन = with blood-smeared mouth; विचिन्त्य = having thought; विचारं विना = without reflection/verification; अक्षिपत् = threw, hurled; पश्चात्तापेन = with remorse; अदह्यत = burned (was consumed); प्रतिक्रियते = is undone, reversed.
Translation: In a certain village lived a brahmin named Devasharma with his wife; they had one infant son and a trusted pet mongoose that guarded the child like a brother. One day the wife took her pot to the river for water and Devasharma went out for alms, leaving the child asleep alone. A black serpent crept from its hole toward the bed; the mongoose leapt on it, fought it and tore it to pieces, saving the child's life. When the wife returned, the joyful mongoose ran to greet her, its mouth smeared with blood. Seeing the blood she thought 'this wicked creature has devoured my son!', became blind with anger, and without a moment's reflection hurled the heavy water-pot upon it, killing it on the spot. Then she entered the house — and saw the child sleeping peacefully, the serpent lying dead in pieces beside the bed. Knowing the truth, she wept aloud, burning with remorse: 'Alas! I have slain the very protector!' But life once gone does not return — a deed done in anger cannot be undone.

नीतिः (Moral): क्रोधः विवेकं नाशयति। Anger destroys विवेक (discrimination): in one blind instant it made a loving mother kill her child's saviour. Act only after verifying the truth (परीक्ष्य कारी भवेत्); a moment of patience can prevent a lifetime of remorse, for anger's deed is irreversible.

क्षमायाः बलम् — The strength of forgiveness (a short episode)

एकस्मिन् आश्रमे कश्चित् शान्तः मुनिः वसति स्म। एकदा कश्चित् दुर्जनः तं निष्कारणं कटुवचनैः निन्दितवान्। मुनिः किमपि न उक्तवान्, केवलं स्मित्वा तूष्णीम् आसीत्। शिष्येण पृष्टः — 'भगवन्, सः भवन्तं निन्दति, भवान् किमर्थं न क्रुध्यति?' मुनिः अवदत् — 'यदि कश्चित् उपहारं ददाति, अहं च न स्वीकरोमि, तर्हि सः उपहारः कस्य भवति? दातुः एव। तथा एव अहम् एतां निन्दां न स्वीकरोमि।' एतत् श्रुत्वा सः दुर्जनः लज्जितः सन् मुनेः क्षमां याचितवान्। एवं क्षमया एव क्रोधः जितः। The sage conquered abuse not by returning it but by refusing to receive it — living proof of the verse अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम्.

नीतिश्लोकाः — Niti verses on क्रोध and क्षमा

क्षमा बलमशक्तानां शक्तानां भूषणं क्षमा ।
क्षमा वशीकृते लोके क्षमया किं न साध्यते ॥
अन्वयः: अशक्तानां क्षमा बलम् (अस्ति)। शक्तानां क्षमा भूषणम् (अस्ति)। क्षमा वशीकृते लोके क्षमया किं न साध्यते?
शब्दार्थः: अशक्तानाम् = of the weak/powerless; बलम् = strength; शक्तानाम् = of the strong/powerful; भूषणम् = ornament; वशीकृते = brought under control, won over; लोके = in the world; साध्यते = is accomplished.
Translation: Forgiveness is the strength of the weak, and forgiveness is the ornament of the strong; when the world is won over by forgiveness, what is there that forgiveness cannot achieve? — For the weak, forbearance is their only real power; for the strong, who COULD retaliate but choose not to, it is a shining ornament. Hence the famous saying क्षमा वीरस्य भूषणम् — 'forgiveness is the hero's ornament.'

अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधमसाधुं साधुना जयेत् ।
जयेत्कदर्यं दानेन जयेत्सत्येन चानृतम् ॥ (महाभारते विदुरनीतिः)
अन्वयः: अक्रोधेन क्रोधं जयेत्। असाधुं साधुना जयेत्। कदर्यं दानेन जयेत्। अनृतं च सत्येन जयेत्।
शब्दार्थः: अक्रोधेन = by non-anger (calmness); जयेत् = one should conquer; असाधुम् = the wicked person; साधुना = by goodness; कदर्यम् = the miser; दानेन = by generosity; अनृतम् = falsehood; सत्येन = by truth.
Translation: Conquer anger by non-anger, the wicked by goodness, the miser by generosity, and falsehood by truth. Vidura's counsel to Dhritarashtra makes the same point as the sage's episode above: anger is defeated not by a greater anger but by its absence.

व्याकरणम् — Grammar from the chapter

(A) विसर्ग-सन्धि (Visarga sandhi). When अः is followed by a voiced sound, the visarga changes. Before the vowel अ, the sequence अः + अ → ओ + ऽ (avagraha replaces the elided अ):
  • क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः → क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः (the chapter title!)
  • क्रोधः + अभिजायते → क्रोधोऽभिजायते (in Gita 2.62)
  • बुद्धिनाशः + अस्ति → बुद्धिनाशोऽस्ति
Before other voiced consonants अः → ओ without avagraha: मनः + रथः → मनोरथः; यशः + धनम् → यशोधनम्; मनः + विकारः → मनोविकारः. Before श/च the visarga becomes श्: कामः + च → कामश्च (compare क्रोधस्तथा = क्रोधः + तथा, where ः → स् before त).

(B) व्यञ्जन-सन्धि (जश्त्व). A final त् becomes द् before a voiced sound: क्रोधात् + भवति → क्रोधाद्भवति; स्मृतिभ्रंशात् + बुद्धिनाशः → स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशः.

(C) समासः. अनर्थकारकः = अनर्थं करोति इति अनर्थकारकः (उपपद-तत्पुरुषः, 'the maker of ruin'). बुद्धिनाशः = बुद्धेः नाशः (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुषः, 'destruction OF the intellect'). स्मृतिविभ्रमः = स्मृतेः विभ्रमः (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुषः).

(D) विभक्तिः. The cascade verses are a parade of पञ्चमी (ablative, 'from'): सङ्गात्, कामात्, क्रोधात्, संमोहात्, स्मृतिभ्रंशात्, बुद्धिनाशात् — each names the SOURCE of the next disaster. Other cases: क्षमया (तृतीया, 'by forgiveness'), अक्रोधेन/दानेन/सत्येन/साधुना (तृतीया, the means of conquest), लोके (सप्तमी, 'in the world'), नरकस्य/आत्मनः (षष्ठी, 'of'), विषयान्/क्रोधम्/अनृतम् (द्वितीया, objects).

(E) लकारः. भवति, उपजायते, सञ्जायते, अभिजायते, प्रणश्यति, साध्यते — all लट् लकार (present tense). त्यजेत्, जयेत् — विधिलिङ् लकार (optative, 'one should...'), the mood of moral counsel.

SUMMARY (सारांशः)

The title क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः (क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः, विसर्ग-सन्धि with अवग्रह) declares that anger is the causer of ruin. The Gita (2.62–63) traces its genealogy: brooding on sense-objects breeds attachment, attachment breeds desire, thwarted desire flares into anger, and anger then destroys the person through delusion, failure of memory and loss of judgement. Gita 16.21 names desire, anger and greed the three-fold gate of hell, to be abandoned. The story of the faithful mongoose shows anger's work in life: one unverified, furious moment killed a saviour and left only irreversible remorse. Against क्रोध the tradition sets क्षमा — the strength of the weak, the ornament of the strong (क्षमा वीरस्य भूषणम्) — and Vidura's rule: conquer anger by non-anger, the wicked by goodness, the miser by giving, falsehood by truth. Grammar learned on the way: विसर्ग-सन्धि (क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः, मनोरथः), जश्त्व (क्रोधाद्भवति), तत्पुरुष समास (अनर्थकारकः, बुद्धिनाशः), the पञ्चमी of source running through the cascade, and the विधिलिङ् of moral counsel (त्यजेत्, जयेत्).

topics.name: क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः — Title, Meaning and Theme
topics.description: The meaning of the chapter title 'क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः' (क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः, joined by विसर्ग-सन्धि with अवग्रह): anger as the causer of ruin (अनर्थ), its place among the six inner enemies (षड्रिपु), and the maxim क्रोधो मूलमनर्थानाम्.

topics.name: गीता-श्लोकौ — The Anger Cascade (Gita 2.62–63 and 16.21)
topics.description: The Bhagavad-Gita's psychological chain: विषय-ध्यान → सङ्ग → काम → क्रोध → संमोह → स्मृतिविभ्रम → बुद्धिनाश → विनाश (2.62–63), and the three gates of hell — काम, क्रोध, लोभ (16.21) — with अन्वय, शब्दार्थ and translation.

topics.name: कथा — The Story of the Mongoose and Hasty Anger
topics.description: An original Sanskrit retelling of the ancient tale of Devasharma's faithful mongoose: how the brahmin's wife, blinded by unverified anger, killed the child's saviour and burned with irreversible remorse — anger destroys विवेक and its deeds cannot be undone.

topics.name: नीतिश्लोकाः — Verses on क्षमा (Forgiveness)
topics.description: Public-domain niti verses on the answering virtue: क्षमा बलमशक्तानां शक्तानां भूषणं क्षमा (forgiveness as the strength of the weak and ornament of the strong), क्षमा वीरस्य भूषणम्, and Vidura's अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम् — conquer anger by non-anger.

topics.name: व्याकरणम् — Sandhi, Samasa, Vibhakti and Lakara
topics.description: Grammar drawn from the chapter: विसर्ग-सन्धि (क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः → क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः, मनोरथः), the अवग्रह sign, जश्त्व (क्रोधाद्भवति), तत्पुरुष समास (अनर्थकारकः, बुद्धिनाशः), the पञ्चमी of source in the cascade, तृतीया of means, and लट् vs विधिलिङ् लकार.

topics.name: शब्दार्थ, Translation and Comprehension
topics.description: Word meanings (शब्दार्थ) of key vocabulary — क्रोधः, क्षमा, संमोहः, स्मृतिः, बुद्धिः, विषयः, सङ्गः, लोभः, नरकः, भूषणम् — and the skill of translating the verses and story passages into simple English and answering comprehension questions.

learning_outcomes.description: Explain the meaning and formation of the title क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः (क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः) and describe the chapter's central theme that anger causes ruin while forgiveness and self-control protect.
Recall and recite Gita 2.62–63 (the anger cascade) and 16.21 (the three gates of hell), reproducing the exact sequence of the chain and the words of the verses.

chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Sanskrit (309) summary for Chapter 19 explains why anger is called the causer of ruin. It traces the Gita's anger cascade (2.62–63), retells the story of the faithful mongoose slain in hasty anger, presents niti verses on क्षमा (forgiveness), and draws out the grammar hidden in the title itself.

sections.heading: The title and the theme
bullets: क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः is formed by विसर्ग-सन्धि: क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः; the sign ऽ (अवग्रह) marks the elided अ of अनर्थकारकः.
अनर्थः (अन् + अर्थः) means calamity or ruin — the opposite of welfare; कारकः means 'the one who causes'. The title thus declares: anger is the causer of ruin.
Tradition counts क्रोध among the six inner enemies (षड्रिपु: काम, क्रोध, लोभ, मोह, मद, मात्सर्य) and calls it the root of calamities — क्रोधो मूलमनर्थानाम्.

sections.heading: The Gita's anger cascade (2.62–63)
bullets: ध्यायतो विषयान्... (2.62): brooding on sense-objects breeds attachment (सङ्ग); attachment breeds desire (काम); thwarted desire flares into anger (क्रोध).

क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः... (2.63): anger produces delusion (संमोह), delusion bewilders memory (स्मृतिविभ्रम), memory-loss destroys judgement (बुद्धिनाश), and with judgement gone the person perishes (प्रणश्यति).
The whole chain runs on the पञ्चमी (ablative) of source: सङ्गात्, कामात्, क्रोधात्, संमोहात्, स्मृतिभ्रंशात्, बुद्धिनाशात् — each stage is the source of the next.
The chain is most easily broken at its first link — by not letting the mind brood on the object of craving — because at the later links clarity is already lost.

sections.heading: Three gates of hell and the story of hasty anger
bullets: Gita 16.21 names desire, anger and greed (कामः क्रोधस्तथा लोभः) the three-fold gate of hell, destructive of the self, and counsels: तस्मादेतत्त्रयं त्यजेत् — abandon this triad.
In the story, Devasharma's faithful mongoose kills a serpent and saves the sleeping child; the returning mother, seeing its blood-smeared mouth, assumes it killed her son.
Blind with anger and without verifying (विचारं विना), she hurls the water-pot and kills the mongoose — then finds the child safe and the snake dead, and burns with remorse (पश्चात्ताप).
Moral: anger destroys विवेक (discrimination); verify before you act (परीक्ष्य कारी भवेत्), for a deed done in anger cannot be undone.

sections.heading: Kshama — the answering virtue
bullets: क्षमा बलमशक्तानां शक्तानां भूषणं क्षमा: forgiveness is the strength of the weak and the ornament of the strong — the strong COULD retaliate but choose not to.
क्षमा वशीकृते लोके क्षमया किं न साध्यते: when the world is won over by forgiveness, nothing remains beyond its reach; hence क्षमा वीरस्य भूषणम्.
Vidura's counsel: अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम् — conquer anger by non-anger, the wicked by goodness, the miser by generosity, falsehood by truth.
The sage's episode shows the method: by refusing to 'accept' the abuse, he left it with the abuser — and his calm turned the abuser to repentance.

sections.heading: Grammar from the chapter
bullets: विसर्ग-सन्धि: अः + अ → ओ + ऽ (क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः, क्रोधोऽभिजायते); अः + voiced consonant → ओ (मनः + रथः = मनोरथः, यशः + धनम् = यशोधनम्); ः → श्/स् before च/त (कामश्च, क्रोधस्तथा).
जश्त्व (व्यञ्जन-सन्धि): a final त् voices to द् — क्रोधात् + भवति = क्रोधाद्भवति; स्मृतिभ्रंशात् + बुद्धिनाशः = स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशः.
समास: अनर्थकारकः = अनर्थं करोति इति (उपपद-तत्पुरुष); बुद्धिनाशः = बुद्धेः नाशः and स्मृतिविभ्रमः = स्मृतेः विभ्रमः (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष).
विभक्ति and लकार: तृतीया of means (क्षमया, अक्रोधेन, दानेन, सत्येन); लट् for present statements (भवति, प्रणश्यति); विधिलिङ् for moral counsel (त्यजेत्, जयेत्).

key_takeaways: The title क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः (क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः, विसर्ग-सन्धि) declares that anger is the causer of ruin — क्रोधो मूलमनर्थानाम्.
Anger is not sudden: it grows link by link — विषय-ध्यान → सङ्ग → काम → क्रोध (Gita 2.62).
Once flared, anger destroys the person step by step: संमोह → स्मृतिविभ्रम → बुद्धिनाश → विनाश (Gita 2.63).
Desire, anger and greed are the three-fold gate of hell (Gita 16.21) — तस्मादेतत्त्रयं त्यजेत्.
The mongoose story warns: verify before acting, for a deed done in blind anger is irreversible and leaves only remorse.
क्षमा is the strength of the weak and the ornament of the strong — क्षमा वीरस्य भूषणम्; conquer anger by non-anger (अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम्).
The grammar of the chapter itself teaches: विसर्ग-सन्धि with अवग्रह, जश्त्व, तत्पुरुष समास, the पञ्चमी of source and the विधिलिङ् of counsel.

glossary.definition: Anger, wrath — one of the six inner enemies (षड्रिपु); the chapter's subject, called the causer of ruin (अनर्थकारक).
Calamity, ruin, disaster — literally 'non-good' (अन् + अर्थः), the opposite of welfare and purpose.
The sign ऽ marking an elided initial अ after a विसर्ग-सन्धि, as in क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः.
A sense-object; a thing of enjoyment on which the mind broods, beginning the anger cascade (ध्यायतो विषयान्).
Attachment, clinging; arises from brooding on sense-objects and gives birth to desire (सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः).
Desire, craving; born of attachment, and when thwarted it flares into anger (कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते).
Delusion, complete mental confusion — the first fruit of anger (क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः).
Bewilderment or wandering of memory; the deluded mind forgets its own lessons and values.
Destruction of the intellect, the power of discrimination (बुद्धेः नाशः, षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष); from it the person perishes.
Greed; with desire and anger it forms the three-fold gate of hell in Gita 16.21.
The gate of hell; Gita 16.21 calls काम, क्रोध and लोभ its three-fold form, destructive of the self.
Forgiveness, forbearance — the strength of the weak, the ornament of the strong, and the hero's ornament (क्षमा वीरस्य भूषणम्).
Mongoose; in the story the faithful guardian that killed the serpent and was slain by the mother's unverified anger.
Remorse, repentance felt after a wrong deed; the mother's burning regret when the truth was known.
The optative mood ('one should...'), used for moral counsel in the verses: त्यजेत्, जयेत्, विवर्जयेत्.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः (NIOS Sanskrit 309, Chapter 19)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Write Sanskrit words in Devanagari and give your explanations in English. Quote the verses from the lesson where needed.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of the chapter title क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः, name the sandhi, and explain what the sign ऽ indicates.
questions.answer: क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः = क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः. This is विसर्ग-सन्धि: when अः is followed by the vowel अ, the sequence becomes ओ and the following अ is elided. The sign ऽ is called अवग्रह; it marks the place of the elided अ of अनर्थकारकः.
questions.explanation: The title itself demonstrates the visarga-sandhi rule अः + अ → ओ + ऽ.

questions.question: Write out, in order, the full chain of the anger cascade taught in Gita 2.62–63, from brooding on sense-objects to final ruin.
questions.answer: विषय-ध्यानम् (brooding on sense-objects) → सङ्गः (attachment) → कामः (desire) → क्रोधः (anger) → संमोहः (delusion) → स्मृतिविभ्रमः (bewilderment of memory) → बुद्धिनाशः (destruction of judgement) → प्रणश्यति (the person perishes).
questions.explanation: 2.62 gives the birth of anger; 2.63 gives its destructive career.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of each: संमोहः, स्मृतिविभ्रमः, बुद्धिनाशः, विषयः, सङ्गः.
questions.answer: संमोहः = delusion, complete confusion; स्मृतिविभ्रमः = bewilderment/wandering of memory; बुद्धिनाशः = destruction of the intellect (judgement); विषयः = sense-object; सङ्गः = attachment.
questions.explanation: All five words come from the cascade of Gita 2.62–63.

questions.question:
Translate into simple English:
क्षमा बलमशक्तानां शक्तानां भूषणं क्षमा ।
क्षमा वशीकृते लोके क्षमया किं न साध्यते ॥
questions.answer: Forgiveness is the strength of the weak, and forgiveness is the ornament of the strong. When the world has been won over by forgiveness, what is there that cannot be accomplished by forgiveness?
questions.explanation: अशक्तानाम् = of the weak; शक्तानाम् = of the strong; वशीकृते लोके = when the world is brought under control; साध्यते = is accomplished.

questions.question: According to Gita 16.21, what are the three gates of hell, and what does the verse counsel us to do?
questions.answer: The three gates of hell (नरकस्य द्वारम्) are कामः (desire), क्रोधः (anger) and लोभः (greed). They are called नाशनमात्मनः — destructive of the self. The verse counsels: तस्मादेतत्त्रयं त्यजेत् — therefore one should abandon this triad.
questions.explanation: त्रिविधं नरकस्येदं द्वारम्... कामः क्रोधस्तथा लोभः.

questions.question: Analyse the anger cascade of Gita 2.62–63 step by step, explaining HOW each link produces the next. Then illustrate the whole chain with one example from a student's daily life, and state where the chain is best broken and why.
questions.answer:
The cascade: (1) ध्यायतो विषयान् — the mind dwells repeatedly on an attractive object; (2) सङ्गः — repetition hardens into attachment; (3) कामः — attachment becomes an active craving to possess; (4) क्रोधः — when the craving is blocked, its energy turns into anger; (5) संमोहः — anger floods the mind and blurs judgement into delusion; (6) स्मृतिविभ्रमः — the deluded person forgets his own values, lessons and resolutions; (7) बुद्धिनाशः — with memory gone, the discriminating intellect collapses; (8) प्रणश्यति — the person acts blindly and is ruined.
Example: a student keeps thinking about a new phone (ध्यान); grows attached to the idea (सङ्ग); begins craving it (काम); when parents refuse, he bursts into rage (क्रोध); in that state he shouts things he does not mean (संमोह), forgets his parents' sacrifices and his own promises (स्मृतिविभ्रम), can no longer judge right from wrong (बुद्धिनाश), and damages his relationships and studies (विनाश).
The chain is best broken at the FIRST link — by not letting the mind brood on the object — because there the mind is still clear and free; at the later links (delusion, memory-loss) the very faculties needed to resist have already been damaged.
questions.explanation: Full-chain analysis + modern illustration + the strategic point that prevention at the first link is easiest.

questions.question: Narrate the story of Devasharma's mongoose in your own words (English or simple Sanskrit) and bring out clearly TWO morals it teaches about anger.
questions.answer:
In a village lived the brahmin Devasharma with his wife, their infant son and a trusted pet mongoose that guarded the child. One day the wife went to the river for water and Devasharma went out for alms, leaving the child asleep. A black serpent crept toward the bed; the mongoose fought it and tore it to pieces, saving the child. When the mother returned, the mongoose ran joyfully to greet her, its mouth smeared with the serpent's blood. Seeing the blood, she concluded it had devoured her son and, blind with anger, hurled the water-pot and killed it on the spot. Inside she found the child sleeping safely beside the dead serpent. She wept with burning remorse — she had slain the very protector of her son.
Morals: (1) Anger destroys विवेक — in one blind moment it turned a loving mother into the killer of her benefactor; never act on appearances without verifying the truth (परीक्ष्य कारी भवेत्). (2) A deed done in anger is irreversible — the mongoose's life, once taken, could not be returned; a moment of patience prevents a lifetime of remorse (पश्चात्ताप).
questions.explanation: Complete narration plus the twin morals of verification and irreversibility.

questions.question: State the विभक्ति (case) and its meaning-role of each word as used in the chapter's verses: क्रोधात्, क्षमया, लोके.
questions.answer: क्रोधात् = पञ्चमी (ablative) → 'from anger' — the source (क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः). क्षमया = तृतीया (instrumental) → 'by forgiveness' — the means (क्षमया किं न साध्यते). लोके = सप्तमी (locative) → 'in the world' — the place (क्षमा वशीकृते लोके).
questions.explanation: पञ्चमी shows source, तृतीया shows means, सप्तमी shows place.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम्. How did the sage in the lesson put this teaching into practice?
questions.answer: अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम् means 'one should conquer anger by non-anger' — an angry attack is defeated not by answering rage but by calmness. The sage, abused without cause, stayed silent and smiling; he explained that an unaccepted gift remains with the giver, and likewise he refused to accept the abuse. His calm forgiveness made the abuser feel ashamed and seek pardon — anger was conquered by non-anger.
questions.explanation: Vidura's verse plus the sage's 'unaccepted gift' episode from the lesson.

questions.question: 'क्षमा is the ornament of the strong, not a sign of weakness.' Do you agree? Give two reasons based on the chapter's verses.
questions.answer: Yes. (1) The verse क्षमा बलमशक्तानां शक्तानां भूषणं क्षमा says forgiveness is an ORNAMENT precisely for the strong — one who has the power to retaliate but chooses restraint shows mastery over himself, which is a higher strength than muscle; hence क्षमा वीरस्य भूषणम्, the HERO'S ornament. (2) क्षमया किं न साध्यते — forgiveness actually achieves what force cannot: it wins over the world (वशीकृते लोके) and, as in the sage's story, transforms even the offender. What conquers more is stronger; therefore क्षमा is strength, not weakness.
questions.explanation: Evaluation supported by both niti verses and the sage's episode.

a bolt from the sky without any cause
the first step of the chain
questions.answer: not sudden — it grows link by link from brooding and craving
questions.explanation: Anger is manufactured by the mind through ध्यान → सङ्ग → काम.

questions.question: A student keeps thinking all day about a classmate's new phone. In the Gita's cascade this corresponds to
questions.explanation: Constant dwelling on the object is the first link of the chain.

the child harmed and the serpent alive
the mongoose hiding under the bed

questions.explanation: क्रोधेन कृतं कर्म न प्रतिक्रियते — a deed done in anger cannot be undone.

questions.explanation: बुद्धिः = the discriminating intellect; बुद्धिनाशः = its destruction.

questions.question: क्षमा बलमशक्तानाम् means
options: forgiveness is the strength of the weak
forgiveness is the weakness of the strong
strength belongs only to the weak
questions.answer: forgiveness is the strength of the weak
questions.explanation: For the powerless, forbearance is their only real power.

questions.question: शक्तानां भूषणं क्षमा means forgiveness is
questions.explanation: One who could retaliate but chooses restraint wears क्षमा as an ornament.

questions.question: क्षमया किं न साध्यते is a rhetorical question meaning

what should be achieved by force?
questions.answer: there is nothing forgiveness cannot achieve
questions.explanation: When the world is won over by क्षमा, everything is within its reach.

questions.question: Why is the क्षमा of the STRONG considered especially praiseworthy?

they never feel anger at all
questions.answer: they have the power to retaliate yet choose restraint
questions.explanation: Forbearance chosen from strength shows self-mastery — hence 'ornament'.

questions.question: क्षमा वीरस्य भूषणम् means

questions.explanation: 'Destruction OF the intellect' — genitive tatpurusha.

questions.explanation: Locative — 'IN the world'.

questions.explanation: The optative ('one should...') — the mood of moral counsel.

questions.explanation: भवति = 'arises/becomes' — present tense, लट् लकार.

questions.question: The correct translation of त्रिविधं नरकस्येदं द्वारं नाशनमात्मनः is

the three worlds are gates of heaven
hell has no gates for the self
the self has three kinds of wealth

questions.explanation: सङ्गः तेषु उपजायते — attachment arises in/toward those objects.

so one should embrace these three
questions.answer: therefore one should abandon this triad
questions.explanation: तस्मात् = therefore; एतत् त्रयम् = this triad; त्यजेत् = one should abandon.

questions.answer: when the world has been won over by forgiveness
questions.explanation: वशीकृते लोके — locative absolute: 'the world having been brought under control'.

an angry deed must be repeated
questions.answer: a deed done in anger cannot be undone
questions.explanation: न प्रतिक्रियते = is not reversed/undone — anger's deed is irreversible.

questions.explanation: It means the opposite — anger is the CAUSER OF RUIN (अनर्थकारक).

questions.question: The title क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः is formed by विसर्ग-सन्धि.
questions.explanation: क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः: अः + अ → ओ + ऽ (avagraha).

questions.question: According to Gita 2.62, anger is born directly from attachment (सङ्ग), without desire in between.
questions.explanation: The order is सङ्गात् कामः, कामात् क्रोधः — desire comes between.

questions.question: Gita 16.21 lists काम, क्रोध and मोह as the three gates of hell.
questions.explanation: The third gate is लोभ (greed), not मोह — कामः क्रोधस्तथा लोभः.

questions.question: In the Gita's cascade, ruin ultimately begins with brooding on sense-objects.
questions.explanation: ध्यायतो विषयान् is the first link from which the whole chain grows.

questions.question: The word संमोहः means 'courage'.
questions.explanation: संमोहः means delusion, complete mental confusion.

questions.question: In the story, the mongoose had actually killed the brahmin's child.
questions.explanation: It had killed the SERPENT and saved the child; the blood was misread.

questions.question: The niti verse calls क्षमा the ornament of the strong.
questions.explanation: शक्तानां भूषणं क्षमा — forgiveness adorns those who could retaliate.

questions.question: The verb त्यजेत् (in तस्मादेतत्त्रयं त्यजेत्) is in लट् लकार.
questions.explanation: त्यजेत् is विधिलिङ् (optative, 'one should abandon'), not present tense.

questions.question: अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम् advises conquering anger by answering it with greater anger.
questions.explanation: It advises the opposite: conquer anger BY NON-ANGER (अक्रोधेन).

questions.question: कामात् ______ अभिजायते। (Gita 2.62)
questions.explanation: From (thwarted) desire anger is born — कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते.

questions.question: क्रोधाद्भवति ______। (Gita 2.63)
questions.explanation: From anger arises delusion.

questions.question: सङ्गात् सञ्जायते ______। (Gita 2.62)
questions.explanation: From attachment desire is born.

questions.question: बुद्धिनाशात् ______। (Gita 2.63 — final word of the verse)
questions.explanation: With the intellect destroyed, the person perishes.

questions.question: कामः क्रोधस्तथा ______ — इति नरकस्य त्रिविधं द्वारम्। (Gita 16.21)
questions.explanation: Desire, anger and GREED are the three gates of hell.

questions.question: शक्तानां भूषणं ______।
questions.explanation: Forgiveness is the ornament of the strong.

questions.question: अक्रोधेन जयेत् ______। (विदुरनीतिः)
questions.explanation: One should conquer anger by non-anger.

questions.question: सन्धिं कुरुत: क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः = ______
questions.explanation: विसर्ग-सन्धि: अः + अ → ओ + ऽ.

questions.question: सन्धिं कुरुत: मनः + रथः = ______
questions.explanation: Visarga after अ becomes ओ before a voiced sound.

questions.question: 'क्रोध' शब्दस्य पञ्चमी-विभक्तेः एकवचनरूपं लिखत: ______ (as in '______ भवति संमोहः')
questions.explanation: पञ्चमी एकवचन of क्रोधः is क्रोधात् ('from anger').

questions.question: The sign ऽ, which marks an elided अ in क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः, is called ______ in Sanskrit.
questions.explanation: The avagraha marks the elision of initial अ after visarga-sandhi.

questions.question: 'Anger' इत्यस्य संस्कृतपदं ______।
questions.explanation: क्रोधः = anger.

questions.question: 'Forgiveness' इत्यस्य संस्कृतपदं ______।
questions.explanation: क्षमा = forgiveness, forbearance.

questions.question: कथायां शिशोः रक्षकः ______ आसीत्। (the animal that saved the child)
questions.explanation: The mongoose (नकुलः) killed the serpent and saved the child.

questions.question: 'Delusion' इति अर्थं वहति गीतायाः पदं ______। (क्रोधाद्भवति ______)
questions.explanation: संमोहः = delusion, the first fruit of anger in Gita 2.63.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of the chapter title क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः, breaking it into its two component words.
questions.answer: The title is क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः joined by विसर्ग-सन्धि. क्रोधः = anger; अनर्थः (अन् + अर्थः) = calamity/ruin, the opposite of welfare; कारकः = the one who causes. So the title declares: 'Anger is the causer of ruin' — anger brings disaster upon the one who harbours it and upon those around him.
questions.explanation: Title = क्रोधः + अनर्थ + कारक with meanings of each element.

questions.question: Why do the wise call क्रोध an अनर्थकारक? Give any three harms of anger mentioned or implied in the chapter.
questions.answer: (1) Anger destroys judgement: through संमोह and स्मृतिविभ्रम it ends in बुद्धिनाश, so the angry person can no longer tell right from wrong (Gita 2.63). (2) It causes irreversible deeds: like the mother who killed the faithful mongoose, one acts before verifying and is left only with remorse. (3) It ruins the self and relationships: Gita 16.21 calls क्रोध a gate of hell, नाशनमात्मनः — destructive of the self; hence क्रोधो मूलमनर्थानाम्, anger is the root of calamities.
questions.explanation: Three harms: loss of judgement, irreversible action, self-destruction.

questions.question: Based on the whole chapter, suggest three practical ways (उपायाः) a student can keep anger under control.
questions.answer: (1) Break the chain at the first link: do not keep brooding on the desired object (ध्यायतो विषयान्) — turn the mind to study, work or service before attachment and craving harden. (2) Verify before reacting: like the lesson of the mongoose story, pause and check the facts (परीक्ष्य कारी भवेत्) before speaking or acting in heat. (3) Practise क्षमा and calm response: answer provocation with non-anger (अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम्), as the sage did by refusing to 'accept' the abuse — calmness disarms the offender and protects one's own mind.
questions.explanation: Prevention (no brooding), verification (story), and kshama (niti verses).

questions.question: Write Gita 2.62 (ध्यायतो विषयान्...) from memory and give its English translation.
questions.answer:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते । सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
Translation: For a man who keeps brooding on sense-objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment is born desire; and from (thwarted) desire anger is born.
questions.explanation: The first verse of the anger cascade with translation.

questions.question: Write Gita 16.21 (त्रिविधं नरकस्य...) and name the three gates of hell with their English meanings.
questions.answer:
त्रिविधं नरकस्येदं द्वारं नाशनमात्मनः । कामः क्रोधस्तथा लोभस्तस्मादेतत्त्रयं त्यजेत् ॥
The three gates of hell are: कामः (desire/craving), क्रोधः (anger) and लोभः (greed). The verse calls them destructive of the self and counsels abandoning all three.
questions.explanation: Verse plus the triad काम-क्रोध-लोभ with meanings.

questions.question: Explain in your own words how each of these three links follows from the previous one: संमोहः → स्मृतिविभ्रमः → बुद्धिनाशः.
questions.answer: संमोहः: anger floods the mind and blurs perception into delusion — the person no longer sees the situation as it is. स्मृतिविभ्रमः: in that deluded state memory fails — one forgets one's own values, past lessons and resolutions ('I will never shout at my parents'), which would otherwise act as brakes. बुद्धिनाशः: with those remembered standards gone, the discriminating intellect collapses — there is nothing left to weigh right against wrong, so the person acts blindly and is ruined (प्रणश्यति).
questions.explanation: Each link removes one more safeguard: perception, memory, judgement.

questions.question: The Gita places काम (desire) before क्रोध (anger). Why is anger said to be born of desire?
questions.answer: Anger is the reaction of a craving mind when its craving is blocked. As long as desire flows unobstructed there is no rage; the moment the desired object is denied or delayed, the energy of the desire turns into fury against the obstacle — कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते. Hence one who reduces craving cuts off anger at its root.
questions.explanation: Thwarted desire converts into anger; no craving, no rage.

questions.question: Where does the lesson say the anger-chain should be broken, and what does this mean in practice for a student?
questions.answer: At the first link — विषय-ध्यानम्, the brooding on the object. In practice this means: when the mind starts circling around a craving (a phone, a rank, a grudge), immediately redirect it to study, play or work instead of feeding the thought. At that stage the mind is still clear; once attachment, craving and anger have formed, the faculties needed to resist (memory, judgement) are themselves being damaged.
questions.explanation: Prevention at the first link is easiest because clarity is intact.

questions.question: Why did the brahmin's wife kill the mongoose, and what was her error of reasoning?
questions.answer: Returning with her water-pot she saw the mongoose run to her with a blood-smeared mouth, and concluded that it had devoured her son. Her error was judging by mere appearance and acting instantly in rage, विचारं विना — without going inside to verify. The blood was in fact the serpent's; the mongoose was the child's saviour.
questions.explanation: Appearance (blood) + unverified inference + instant rage = fatal error.

questions.question: What did the mother discover inside the house, and what feeling followed? Quote the Sanskrit word for that feeling.
questions.answer: She found her child sleeping safely and the serpent lying dead in pieces beside the bed — proof that the mongoose had saved, not harmed, her son. She was consumed by remorse — पश्चात्तापः (महता पश्चात्तापेन अदह्यत) — weeping that she had slain the very protector.
questions.explanation: Truth discovered too late; पश्चात्ताप = remorse.

questions.question: Connect the mongoose story to the Gita's cascade: which links of 2.62–63 can you identify in the mother's conduct?
questions.answer: Her fierce attachment (सङ्ग) to her child and the desire (काम) for his safety were suddenly 'thwarted' by the sight of blood, and flared instantly into क्रोध. Anger produced संमोह — she was deluded into seeing the saviour as the killer; स्मृतिविभ्रम — she forgot the mongoose's long faithfulness; बुद्धिनाश — her judgement collapsed and she struck without verifying; and the result was ruin (विनाश) — the guardian dead and herself burning in remorse. The story is the cascade enacted in a single minute.
questions.explanation: The tale maps link-by-link onto Gita 2.62–63.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of: ध्यायतः, विषयान्, सङ्गः, कामः, अभिजायते.
questions.answer: ध्यायतः = of one brooding/contemplating; विषयान् = sense-objects (accusative plural); सङ्गः = attachment; कामः = desire, craving; अभिजायते = is born, springs up.
questions.explanation: All five words are from Gita 2.62.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: अशक्तानाम्, शक्तानाम्, भूषणम्, वशीकृते, साध्यते.
questions.answer: अशक्तानाम् = of the weak/powerless; शक्तानाम् = of the strong/powerful; भूषणम् = ornament; वशीकृते = brought under control, won over; साध्यते = is accomplished/achieved.
questions.explanation: All five words are from the क्षमा verse.

questions.question: Explain the meaning of the verse क्षमा बलमशक्तानां शक्तानां भूषणं क्षमा, bringing out the two different roles क्षमा plays.
questions.answer: For the weak (अशक्त), forgiveness is their बल — strength: unable to retaliate, their forbearance preserves their dignity and peace and is their only real power. For the strong (शक्त), forgiveness is a भूषण — ornament: they possess the power to punish, yet choosing restraint displays self-mastery, which adorns their strength as a jewel adorns the body. The second half adds: a world won over by forgiveness leaves nothing that क्षमा cannot achieve.
questions.explanation: Same virtue, two roles: strength for the weak, ornament for the strong.

questions.question: Write the four 'conquests' taught in Vidura's verse अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम्... with their English meanings.
questions.answer: (1) अक्रोधेन जयेत् क्रोधम् — conquer anger by non-anger (calmness). (2) असाधुं साधुना जयेत् — conquer the wicked by goodness. (3) जयेत् कदर्यं दानेन — conquer the miser by generosity. (4) जयेत् सत्येन च अनृतम् — conquer falsehood by truth. In each pair the vice is defeated not by its own kind but by its opposite virtue.
questions.explanation: Four vices, four opposite virtues — the principle of conquest by opposites.

questions.question: Retell briefly the sage's episode from the lesson and state what it proves about the power of क्षमा.
questions.answer: A wicked man abused a peaceful sage without cause. The sage stayed silent and smiling. Asked by his disciple why he did not grow angry, he replied: 'If someone offers a gift and I do not accept it, with whom does the gift remain? With the giver. In the same way I do not accept this abuse.' Hearing this, the abuser was ashamed and begged forgiveness. It proves that क्षमा is an active power, not passivity: by refusing to receive the provocation the sage kept his own mind unshaken AND transformed the offender — anger was conquered by non-anger (अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम्).
questions.explanation: The 'unaccepted gift' argument shows forgiveness defeating anger.

questions.question: State the विसर्ग-सन्धि rule seen in the chapter title, and apply it to join: (a) क्रोधः + अभिजायते (b) बुद्धिनाशः + अस्ति (c) मनः + विकारः.
questions.answer: Rule: a visarga preceded by अ, when followed by the vowel अ, becomes ओ and the following अ is elided, its place marked by अवग्रह (ऽ); before other voiced sounds अः simply becomes ओ. (a) क्रोधः + अभिजायते = क्रोधोऽभिजायते. (b) बुद्धिनाशः + अस्ति = बुद्धिनाशोऽस्ति. (c) मनः + विकारः = मनोविकारः (no avagraha, since विकारः begins with a consonant).
questions.explanation: अः + अ → ओ + ऽ; अः + voiced consonant → ओ.

questions.question: Give the विग्रह (dissolution) and name the समास of: (a) अनर्थकारकः (b) बुद्धिनाशः (c) स्मृतिविभ्रमः.
questions.answer: (a) अनर्थकारकः = अनर्थं करोति इति अनर्थकारकः — उपपद-तत्पुरुषः ('the maker of ruin'). (b) बुद्धिनाशः = बुद्धेः नाशः — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुषः ('destruction of the intellect'). (c) स्मृतिविभ्रमः = स्मृतेः विभ्रमः — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुषः ('bewilderment of memory').
questions.explanation: One upapada-tatpurusha and two genitive tatpurushas from the chapter.

questions.question: The cascade verses use a series of पञ्चमी forms. List any four of them and state what the पञ्चमी expresses there.
questions.answer: Any four of: सङ्गात्, कामात्, क्रोधात्, संमोहात्, स्मृतिभ्रंशात्, बुद्धिनाशात्. The पञ्चमी (ablative) expresses the SOURCE — 'from': each stage is the source from which the next disaster arises (e.g. कामात् क्रोधः — from desire, anger).
questions.explanation: The ablative of source strings the whole chain together.

questions.question: Translate Gita 2.63 into simple English: क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः । स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥
questions.answer: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, bewilderment of memory; from the failure of memory, destruction of the intellect; and when the intellect is destroyed, the person perishes utterly.
questions.explanation: Four clauses, each with a पञ्चमी of source driving the next stage.

questions.question: Translate this line from the story: सा विचारं विना एव जलपूर्णं घटं नकुलस्य उपरि अक्षिपत्।
questions.answer: Without any reflection (verification) at all, she hurled the water-filled pot upon the mongoose.
questions.explanation: विचारं विना = without reflection; जलपूर्णं घटम् = water-filled pot; अक्षिपत् = threw.

questions.question: Write the अन्वय (prose order) of Gita 2.62 and then translate it.
questions.answer:
अन्वयः: विषयान् ध्यायतः पुंसः तेषु सङ्गः उपजायते । सङ्गात् कामः सञ्जायते । कामात् क्रोधः अभिजायते ।
Translation: For a man brooding on sense-objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment desire is born; from desire anger is born.
questions.explanation: Anvaya rearranges the verse into natural prose order before translating.

questions.question: 'क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः' — justify the chapter's title with reference to (a) its grammatical formation, (b) the Gita's analysis, and (c) one example from life or the lesson's story.
questions.answer:
(a) Formation: क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः joined by विसर्ग-सन्धि (अः + अ → ओ + ऽ, the elision marked by अवग्रह). अनर्थ = ruin (अन् + अर्थ, 'non-good'); कारक = causer; so the title itself asserts: anger is the manufacturer of calamity — echoing the maxim क्रोधो मूलमनर्थानाम्.
(b) The Gita's analysis (2.62–63) proves the claim psychologically: anger, itself born of brooding, attachment and thwarted desire, then destroys the person in stages — delusion (संमोह), failure of memory (स्मृतिविभ्रम), collapse of judgement (बुद्धिनाश), and utter ruin (प्रणश्यति). Gita 16.21 seals it by naming क्रोध a gate of hell, destructive of the self.
(c) Example: the brahmin's wife, blind with one minute of unverified rage, killed the mongoose that had saved her child — gaining nothing and losing a faithful guardian, with only पश्चात्ताप left. In grammar, scripture and life alike, anger is truly अनर्थकारक.
questions.explanation: Title justified from sandhi, from Gita 2.62–63 and 16.21, and from the story.

questions.question: Write both cascade verses (Gita 2.62 and 2.63) with their अन्वय and English translation.
questions.answer:
Verse 2.62: ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते । सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
अन्वयः: विषयान् ध्यायतः पुंसः तेषु सङ्गः उपजायते; सङ्गात् कामः सञ्जायते; कामात् क्रोधः अभिजायते।
Translation: For a man brooding on sense-objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment desire is born; from desire anger is born.
Verse 2.63: क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः । स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥
अन्वयः: क्रोधात् संमोहः भवति; संमोहात् स्मृतिविभ्रमः; स्मृतिभ्रंशात् बुद्धिनाशः; बुद्धिनाशात् (सः) प्रणश्यति।
Translation: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, bewilderment of memory; from memory's failure, destruction of the intellect; and with the intellect destroyed, the person perishes.
questions.explanation: Both verses reproduced with anvaya and translation.

questions.question: The Gita's anger cascade has been called 'the psychology of self-destruction in eight steps'. Analyse all eight steps, showing the inner logic of each transition, and explain why prevention is superior to cure in this chain.
questions.answer:
(1) विषय-ध्यानम्: the mind repeatedly dwells on an attractive object — apparently harmless daydreaming. (2) सङ्गः: repetition wears a groove; the mind now clings to the object. (3) कामः: clinging becomes active craving — 'I must have it.' (4) क्रोधः: the world inevitably blocks some cravings; the blocked craving's energy converts into anger at the obstacle. (5) संमोहः: anger floods perception; the person no longer sees facts as they are. (6) स्मृतिविभ्रमः: delusion cuts access to memory — values, promises and lessons that would restrain him are forgotten. (7) बुद्धिनाशः: without remembered standards, the discriminating intellect collapses; right and wrong become indistinguishable. (8) प्रणश्यति: the person acts blindly and destroys himself — relationships, reputation, even life.
Prevention is superior to cure because the chain progressively destroys the very faculties needed to stop it: at step 1 the mind is clear and free, and simply redirecting attention costs little; by steps 5–7 perception, memory and judgement — the only tools of self-correction — are themselves disabled. Hence the wise guard the first thought, not the last act.
questions.explanation: Eight-step analysis plus the strategic argument for early prevention.

questions.question: Narrate the full story of the mongoose (नकुलस्य कथा) as given in the lesson, and conclude with its moral in both Sanskrit and English.
questions.answer:
In a village lived the brahmin Devasharma with his wife, their infant son, and a trusted mongoose that guarded the child like a brother. One day the wife took her pot to the river for water; Devasharma too went out for alms, leaving the child asleep alone. A black serpent slid from its hole toward the bed. The mongoose leapt up, fought the serpent and tore it to pieces, saving the child's life. When the mother returned, the delighted mongoose ran to greet her with its mouth smeared in the serpent's blood. Seeing the blood she thought, 'This wicked creature has eaten my son!' Blind with anger, without a moment's verification she hurled the heavy water-pot on the mongoose and killed it. Entering the house she found the child sleeping peacefully and the serpent lying dead in pieces. Realising she had slain her son's saviour, she wept aloud, consumed by remorse — but life once gone does not return.
Moral (Sanskrit): क्रोधः विवेकं नाशयति; क्रोधेन कृतं कर्म न प्रतिक्रियते।
Moral (English): Anger destroys discrimination, and a deed done in anger cannot be undone — therefore verify the truth and master your anger before you act.
questions.explanation: Complete narration with bilingual moral.

questions.question: Prepare a glossary of ten key Sanskrit words of this chapter (five from the Gita verses, five from the story or niti verses), giving the English meaning of each and using any two of them in short Sanskrit sentences.
questions.answer:
From the Gita verses: (1) विषयः = sense-object; (2) सङ्गः = attachment; (3) संमोहः = delusion; (4) स्मृतिविभ्रमः = bewilderment of memory; (5) बुद्धिनाशः = destruction of judgement.
From the story and niti verses: (6) नकुलः = mongoose; (7) पश्चात्तापः = remorse; (8) क्षमा = forgiveness; (9) भूषणम् = ornament; (10) अनृतम् = falsehood.
Sentences: क्रोधात् संमोहः भवति। (From anger delusion arises.) क्षमा शक्तानां भूषणम् अस्ति। (Forgiveness is the ornament of the strong.)
questions.explanation: Ten-word glossary plus two original usage sentences.

questions.question: 'Forgiveness is not weakness but the highest strength.' Evaluate this statement in the light of the two niti verses of the chapter and the sage's episode. Also mention one situation where forbearance must be combined with firmness.
questions.answer:
The verse क्षमा बलमशक्तानां शक्तानां भूषणं क्षमा already refutes the equation of forgiveness with weakness: for the powerless it IS their strength, and for the powerful — who could crush the offender — restraint is an ornament, proof of self-mastery. The rhetorical climax क्षमया किं न साध्यते claims forgiveness achieves what force cannot: it wins the world over (वशीकृते लोके). Vidura's अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम् shows the mechanism — anger feeds on counter-anger and starves before calmness. The sage's episode demonstrates it: by refusing to 'accept' the abuse like an unaccepted gift, he remained untouched and the abuser himself was transformed into repentance — a double victory no retaliation could have won. Conquest is the mark of strength, and क्षमा conquers both one's own mind and the opponent's; therefore it is strength of the highest order.
Yet forbearance is not limitless license: where injustice harms the weak — e.g. bullying of a junior student — क्षमा for the offender must be combined with firm, calm action to stop the wrong. Forgiveness renounces hatred, not duty.
questions.explanation: Evaluation from both verses and the episode, with the limit-case of firmness.

questions.question: Write a note on विसर्ग-सन्धि as taught in this chapter: state the rules with the title example, give four more examples (जोड़ें/split), explain the अवग्रह, and add one जश्त्व example from the verses.
questions.answer:
विसर्ग-सन्धि: (Rule 1) अः + अ → ओ + ऽ: the visarga-sequence becomes ओ and the following अ is elided, marked by अवग्रह — क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः = क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः (the title), क्रोधः + अभिजायते = क्रोधोऽभिजायते, बुद्धिनाशः + अस्ति = बुद्धिनाशोऽस्ति. (Rule 2) अः + voiced consonant → ओ, no avagraha — मनः + रथः = मनोरथः, यशः + धनम् = यशोधनम्. (Rule 3) ः → श् before च/छ and स् before त/थ — कामः + च = कामश्च; क्रोधः + तथा = क्रोधस्तथा (Gita 16.21).
The अवग्रह (ऽ) is purely a written sign: it is not pronounced, but shows the reader that an initial अ has been elided, enabling correct सन्धि-विच्छेद.
जश्त्व example: क्रोधात् + भवति = क्रोधाद्भवति (final त् voices to द् before the voiced भ्); similarly स्मृतिभ्रंशात् + बुद्धिनाशः = स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशः.
questions.explanation: Three visarga rules + avagraha + jashtva, all exemplified from the chapter.

questions.question: Compose a short bilingual reflection (5–6 Sanskrit sentences with English translation) titled 'क्रोधं त्यजामि, क्षमां भजामि' ('I abandon anger, I embrace forgiveness'), using vocabulary and ideas from this chapter.
questions.answer:
क्रोधः अनर्थकारकः अस्ति। (Anger is the causer of ruin.)
क्रोधात् संमोहः भवति, संमोहात् बुद्धिः नश्यति। (From anger comes delusion; from delusion the intellect perishes.)
अतः अहं विषयाणां ध्यानं न करोमि। (Therefore I do not brood over objects of craving.)
यदा कोपः आगच्छति, तदा अहं क्षणं तूष्णीं भवामि, सत्यं च परीक्षे। (When anger comes, I stay silent a moment and verify the truth.)
अक्रोधेन क्रोधं जयामि। (I conquer anger by non-anger.)
क्षमा एव मम बलं भूषणं च। (Forgiveness alone is my strength and my ornament.)
questions.explanation: Original composition weaving the cascade, the story's lesson and the niti verses.

questions.question:
Read the verses and answer:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते । सङ्गात्सञ्जायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः । स्मृतिभ्रंशाद्बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति ॥
(a) List the complete chain in order, in Sanskrit. (b) At which link should a student break the chain, and why there?
questions.answer:
(a) विषय-ध्यानम् → सङ्गः → कामः → क्रोधः → संमोहः → स्मृतिविभ्रमः → बुद्धिनाशः → विनाशः (प्रणश्यति).
(b) At the first link, विषय-ध्यानम् — by not letting the mind brood on the object. There the mind is still clear and free to redirect itself; at the later links the faculties needed to resist (perception, memory, judgement) are progressively destroyed, so stopping becomes nearly impossible.
questions.explanation: The passage-based question tests the chain and the strategy of early prevention.

questions.question:
Case: Ravi wanted the class trophy badly and thought about it day and night. When his friend Amit won it instead, Ravi flew into a rage, shouted insults he never intended, forgot years of friendship, tore up his own notes and failed the next test.
Map each event of this case to the corresponding link of the Gita's anger cascade (2.62–63).
questions.answer: Thinking about the trophy day and night = विषय-ध्यानम् / सङ्गः (brooding hardening into attachment); wanting it badly = कामः (craving); rage when Amit won (desire thwarted) = क्रोधः; shouting insults he never intended = संमोहः (delusion); forgetting years of friendship = स्मृतिविभ्रमः (failure of memory); tearing up his own notes = बुद्धिनाशः (judgement destroyed — acting against his own interest); failing the test / losing friend and marks = प्रणश्यति (ruin).
questions.explanation: A modern case mapped link-by-link onto the cascade.

questions.question:
Read this passage from the story and answer:
रक्तं दृष्ट्वा ब्राह्मणी 'अनेन दुष्टेन मम पुत्रः भक्षितः!' इति विचिन्त्य क्रोधेन अन्धा अभवत्। सा विचारं विना एव जलपूर्णं घटं नकुलस्य उपरि अक्षिपत्।
(a) Translate the passage. (b) Which single Sanskrit phrase here names the mother's real fault?
questions.answer:
(a) Translation: Seeing the blood, the brahmin's wife thought, 'My son has been devoured by this wicked creature!' and became blind with anger. Without any reflection at all, she hurled the water-filled pot upon the mongoose.
(b) The phrase विचारं विना ('without reflection/verification') names her real fault — she acted on an unverified inference while blinded by rage.
questions.explanation: Translation plus identification of the key phrase विचारं विना.

questions.question:
Case: Meera returned home to find her project file torn and ink spilt on her desk. Assuming her younger brother did it, she slapped him in fury. Later she discovered the pet cat had knocked over the shelf.
Which lesson of the mongoose story did Meera ignore, and what should she have done?
questions.answer: She ignored the story's central lesson: never act in anger on mere appearances without verifying the truth (विचारं विना न कार्यं कुर्यात् — परीक्ष्य कारी भवेत्). Like the brahmin's wife she judged from circumstantial evidence (the torn file) and struck an innocent. She should have paused, controlled the surge of anger, asked and examined what actually happened — and only then responded; for a deed done in anger (the slap, like the mongoose's death) cannot be recalled.
questions.explanation: Modern parallel of the story: unverified anger wrongs the innocent.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
त्रिविधं नरकस्येदं द्वारं नाशनमात्मनः । कामः क्रोधस्तथा लोभस्तस्मादेतत्त्रयं त्यजेत् ॥
(a) Name the three gates of hell in Sanskrit. (b) What two things does the verse say about this triad?
questions.answer:
(a) कामः (desire), क्रोधः (anger), लोभः (greed).
(b) The verse says (i) this triad is the three-fold gate of hell (नरकस्य त्रिविधं द्वारम्) and is destructive of the self (नाशनम् आत्मनः); (ii) therefore one should abandon all three (तस्मात् एतत् त्रयं त्यजेत्).
questions.explanation: Direct comprehension of Gita 16.21.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
क्षमा बलमशक्तानां शक्तानां भूषणं क्षमा । क्षमा वशीकृते लोके क्षमया किं न साध्यते ॥
The verse seems paradoxical — the SAME quality is 'strength' for one group and 'ornament' for another. Resolve the paradox: why is क्षमा strength for the weak but ornament for the strong?
questions.answer: For the weak (अशक्त), who cannot retaliate anyway, forgiveness converts their helplessness into dignity: instead of burning in impotent rage they retain peace and moral height — forbearance is the only power actually available to them, hence their बल. For the strong (शक्त), who CAN punish, forgiveness is not necessity but choice; voluntarily renouncing revenge displays mastery over their own anger, a rarer strength than physical power, and so it adorns them as a भूषण — like a jewel that only the wealthy can afford to wear. The paradox dissolves: क्षमा empowers the powerless and beautifies the powerful, and thus (line 2) there is nothing in the world it cannot accomplish.
questions.explanation: The resolution turns on necessity vs choice — availability of retaliation.

questions.question:
Case: During assembly a junior mocked the school captain loudly. The captain, though powerful enough to punish him, smiled, spoke to him kindly in private, and won him over; the junior became his admirer.
Which two sayings from the chapter did the captain's conduct embody? Explain briefly.
questions.answer: (1) शक्तानां भूषणं क्षमा / क्षमा वीरस्य भूषणम् — though strong enough to punish, the captain chose restraint, wearing forgiveness as the ornament of the strong. (2) अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधम् (and असाधुं साधुना जयेत्) — he conquered the junior's rudeness not by counter-anger but by calmness and goodness, actually winning him over (क्षमया किं न साध्यते).
questions.explanation: The captain enacts both niti verses: restraint of the strong, conquest by non-anger.

questions.question:
Read the verse and give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of the four underlined words:
अक्रोधेन जयेत् क्रोधम् असाधुं साधुना जयेत् । जयेत् कदर्यं दानेन जयेत् सत्येन च अनृतम् ॥
Words: अक्रोधेन, असाधुम्, कदर्यम्, अनृतम्.
questions.answer: अक्रोधेन = by non-anger (by calmness); असाधुम् = the wicked person; कदर्यम् = the miser; अनृतम् = falsehood, untruth.
questions.explanation: Four vocabulary items from Vidura's verse of the four conquests.

questions.question:
Read the two forms taken from the chapter: (i) क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः (the title) (ii) क्रोधाद्भवति (Gita 2.63).
For each: do the सन्धि-विच्छेद, name the sandhi/change involved, and state the rule in one line.
questions.answer:
(i) क्रोधोऽनर्थकारकः = क्रोधः + अनर्थकारकः — विसर्ग-सन्धि. Rule: visarga after अ, followed by the vowel अ, becomes ओ and the following अ is elided, marked by अवग्रह (ऽ).
(ii) क्रोधाद्भवति = क्रोधात् + भवति — व्यञ्जन-सन्धि (जश्त्व). Rule: a word-final त् becomes the voiced द् before a voiced sound (here भ्).
questions.explanation: One visarga-sandhi and one jashtva split, each with its rule.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
अक्रोधेन जयेत्क्रोधमसाधुं साधुना जयेत् । जयेत्कदर्यं दानेन जयेत्सत्येन चानृतम् ॥
(a) Translate all four quarters into English. (b) Which लकार is जयेत्, and what nuance does it give the verse?
questions.answer:
(a) Translation: One should conquer anger by non-anger; one should conquer the wicked by goodness; one should conquer the miser by generosity; and one should conquer falsehood by truth.
(b) जयेत् is विधिलिङ् (optative). It gives the nuance of counsel or moral prescription — 'one SHOULD conquer' — stating not a mere fact but a duty recommended to every person.
questions.explanation: Full translation plus the force of the optative in niti literature.
